headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an overall effect size of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.77–0.95), suggesting that total dietary fiber intake is associated with a lower risk of bladder cancer. These findings were supported by low between-study heterogeneity (I² = 0.00%), indicating consistent findings across the included studies.

studies.Population: Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial participants free of cancer at baseline
studies.Ethnicity Basis: NA: no field-specific ethnicity evidence was available
studies.Reference: Dietary fiber intake and the risk of bladder cancer in the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian (PLCO) cohort.
studies.comparison_type: highest versus lowest tertile of total fiber intake
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: completed both the baseline questionnaire and the diet history questionnaire

sample_size.excerpt: A total of 101 721 participants were included in this study as they completed both the baseline questionnaire and the diet history questionnaire (cancer free before completion of the diet history questionnaire).

cases.excerpt: After a median of 12.5 years of follow-up, 776 new cases of bladder cancer were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: Higher intake of total fiber, insoluble fiber and soluble fiber were not significantly associated with a reduced risk of bladder cancer. The multi-adjusted HRs (95 CIs) of highest versus lowest tertile of intake were 0.83 (0.66-1.04) for total fiber (P for trend = 0.098), 0.83 (95% CI: 0.67-1.03) for insoluble fiber (P for trend = 0.092) and 0.86 (95% CI: 0.68-1.08) for soluble fiber (P for trend = 0.168), respectively.

studies.Population: BLEND international consortium participants from 13 prospective cohorts
studies.Ethnicity Supporting Text: The majority (99.3%) of participants were Caucasian.
studies.Reference: Grain and dietary fiber intake and bladder cancer risk: a pooled analysis of prospective cohort studies.
studies.Authors: Yu EYW, Wesselius A, Mehrkanoon S, Brinkman M, van den Brandt P, White E, Weiderpass E, Le Calvez-Kelm F, Gunter M, Huybrechts I, Liedberg F, Skeie G, Tjonneland A, Riboli E, Giles GG, Milne RL, Zeegers MP
studies.Journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Total intakes of dietary fiber and dietary fiber from cereal, fruit, and vegetables were calculated by multiplying the amount of each food consumed by the dietary fiber content per gram according to the USDA.

sample_size.excerpt: We pooled individual data from 574,726 participants in 13 cohort studies, 3214 of whom developed incident BC.

cases.excerpt: In total, 574,726 study participants contributed 6,335,667 person-years of follow-up over a median of 11 y, with 3214 incident BC cases (2416 males, 798 females) diagnosed.

effect_size.excerpt: Intake of total dietary fiber was also inversely associated with BC risk (comparing highest with lowest intake tertile: HR: 0.86; 95% CI: 0.76, 0.98; HR per 1-SD increment: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.82, 0.98; P for trend: 0.021).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Intake of total dietary fiber was also inversely associated with BC risk (comparing highest with lowest intake tertile: HR: 0.86; 95% CI: 0.76, 0.98; HR per 1-SD increment: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.82, 0.98; P for trend: 0.021).

p_value.excerpt: Intake of total dietary fiber was also inversely associated with BC risk (comparing highest with lowest intake tertile: HR: 0.86; 95% CI: 0.76, 0.98; HR per 1-SD increment: 0.91; 95% CI: 0.82, 0.98; P for trend: 0.021).

design.excerpt: Thirteen cohort studies with a total of 574,726 participants, 3214 of whom developed incident BC, had sufficient information on grain intake to be eligible for inclusion in the present study

timing.excerpt: We therefore assessed associations with BC risk for intakes of whole grains and refined grains, using data from 13 prospective cohort studies pooled in the BLEND (BLadder cancer Epidemiology and Nutritional Determinants) international study.

ethnicity.excerpt: The majority (99.3%) of participants were Caucasian.
